3. Subsurface Aeration and Climate-Control Agronomy
Every championship green receives a SubAir vacuum-and-pressure module. Excess moisture is pulled down during heavy rain. Warm air is pushed through the rootzone during frost. Glycol heating loops under primary tournament greens prevent winter dormancy stress and guarantee spring green-up. Thousands of soil-moisture sensors feed a centralized irrigation controller so every sprinkler head waters to the square yard, not the acre. Fertigation injects liquid nutrition and amendments through the same irrigation ring. This is how bentgrass survives July in Washington and still rolls at tournament speed in September.
4. Heavy Earthworks Logistics and Site Preparation
The single-access geometry of Hains Point demands disciplined logistics. Reinforced entryways, erosion control, temporary haul roads, and on-site processing plants keep construction traffic from destroying the park and the surrounding municipal infrastructure. The work is sequenced so public perimeter access is maintained wherever possible during construction.

PHASE TWO
SPECTATOR INFRASTRUCTURE, PUBLIC ACCESS GRIDS, SECURITY ARCHITECTURE, AND MAINTENANCE FLEET LOGISTICS
1. Spectator Hospitality and Major Event Infrastructure
Holes 9, 14, 15, and 18 receive permanent utility hookups—power, fiber, water, sewage—and reinforced pads for multi-tier hospitality chalets and international broadcast compounds. Permanent upscale food-and-beverage pavilions in stone and timber serve both tournament crowds and everyday park visitors. Climate-controlled comfort stations tie into municipal sewer via lift stations. Tensile shade canopies, misting systems, and covered pavilions protect spectators from mid-Atlantic heat. ADA-compliant pedestrian overpasses separate foot traffic from live fairways. Dedicated transformer substations and redundant generator ties power global broadcast compounds. Grandstand foundations around finishing holes are engineered for wind load and maximum occupancy.
2. Public-First Accessibility and Community Infrastructure
Outside tournament windows the entire peninsula remains open, accessible, and discounted under municipal green-fee structures. A reconstructed 12-foot perimeter track of reinforced permeable pavers is physically separated from golf operations by grade-separated berms, landscaping, and acoustic baffling. Solar LED lighting at 100-foot intervals runs off-grid on photovoltaic panels and subterranean lithium storage. Bronze and stainless interpretive plaques and digital kiosks tell the ecological and civic history of Hains Point. A community learning center and junior training pavilion inside the clubhouse complex offers subsidized rentals, clinics, and tutoring space for District youth. ADA parking and transit loops connect to the clubhouse plaza.
This is not an afterthought. It is the political and moral condition of the project. Championship golf on federal land that locks the public out will not stand. Championship golf that the public can still play on Monday morning will become a national model.
3. Advanced Security Architecture and Asset Protection
An 8-foot ornamental black steel fence encloses the peninsula, backed by biometric gates, crash-rated bollards, and hydraulic wedge barriers. Thermal and optical PTZ cameras, ALPR, and facial-recognition nodes operate 24/7. A hardened on-site command bunker has redundant power, direct law-enforcement dispatch, and medical triage bays. Fiber-optic seismic and acoustic cable along the fence line detects climbing, cutting, or tunneling. Marine sonar and thermal buoys watch the Potomac and Washington Channel approaches. The system is sized for both quiet public days and national-security tournament weeks.

text:
RENEWABLE DIESEL, BIODIESEL AND UCO IMPLICATIONS

The Green Markets alert contains no UCO price, supply, carbon-intensity or margin data. The UCO conclusions arise from the interaction between SREs, D4 RIN values and renewable diesel economics rather than from explicit statements in the source. The immediate directional effect is negative for the maximum price renewable diesel and biodiesel producers can pay for UCO, tallow, distillers corn oil and vegetable oils, holding all other credits and product prices constant.

Renewable diesel generally generates approximately 1.6 to 1.7 RINs per gallon, while biodiesel generally generates approximately 1.5 RINs per gallon. A $0.50 decline in D4 price reduces gross RIN revenue by approximately $0.80 to $0.85 per gallon of renewable diesel and approximately $0.75 per gallon of biodiesel. At a D4 price of $1.92, gross RIN value is approximately $3.07 to $3.26 per gallon for renewable diesel and approximately $2.88 per gallon for biodiesel. These values are not operating margins because feedstock, hydrogen, natural gas, catalyst, logistics, yield losses, coproducts, tax credits and low-carbon fuel credits remain material. 

The 1st-order UCO response should be a lower prompt feedstock bid, particularly for marginal volumes delivered to plants with weak non-RIN incentives or limited operational flexibility. Producers can respond through lower run rates, reduced spot procurement, substitution toward cheaper feedstocks, temporary margin compression or a narrower feedstock premium. The burden will not necessarily be passed through immediately because renewable diesel plants often have committed supply agreements, minimum operating requirements, product offtake contracts and substantial fixed costs.

Low-carbon UCO can retain a relative premium even as the outright feedstock complex weakens. UCO’s lower carbon intensity can generate greater value under state low-carbon fuel programs and federal clean-fuel incentives than higher-carbon soybean oil or other virgin vegetable oils. A decline in D4 therefore reduces the common RIN component of feedstock value but does not eliminate carbon-intensity differentiation. The likely result is weaker prompt UCO pricing and producer margins, with greater resilience in the low-carbon premium than in the absolute commodity price.

The physical production response may be slower than the RIN price response. EIA’s 2026 outlook anticipated substantial growth in renewable diesel and biodiesel production, reflecting new capacity and the elevated credit environment prevailing earlier in the year. Plants with positive contribution margins after all credits may continue running despite lower D4 values, while less advantaged units reduce utilization. The marginal production loss should be concentrated among high-cost facilities, plants with expensive feedstock logistics and units lacking strong low-carbon market access. 

The medium-term UCO implication reverses if the 770 million reallocation is finalized with a material biomass-based diesel or advanced component. Higher 2026 and 2027 D4 demand would support renewable diesel utilization and restore feedstock purchasing capacity. The likely temporal pattern is therefore weaker prompt UCO demand and margins, followed by potential deferred stabilization. The magnitude depends on the year split, category split, RIN-bank drawdown and availability of domestic and imported low-carbon feedstocks.

The decision can also alter project economics. New renewable diesel projects are most exposed when projected returns rely heavily on elevated D4 values and aggressive feedstock assumptions. A volatile exemption regime increases the required return on capital, reduces confidence in long-dated RIN curves and makes low-carbon credit diversification more valuable. Existing plants with low capital intensity, advantaged hydrogen integration, secure low-cost feedstocks and access to multiple credit regimes should outperform greenfield projects dependent on a narrow RIN revenue stack.

ETHANOL AND CONVENTIONAL BIOFUEL IMPLICATIONS

D6 prices should experience a larger relative effect than physical ethanol demand. E10 blending is deeply embedded in the gasoline system and can remain economical because ethanol contributes octane and can trade below gasoline blendstock on an energy-adjusted or octane-adjusted basis. Small-refinery exemptions can therefore reduce D6 retirement demand without causing an equivalent reduction in ethanol blending. The price response can be concentrated in the compliance credit rather than the underlying ethanol gallon.

The physical impact becomes more significant near the conventional blend wall. Higher future total RVOs cannot be satisfied indefinitely through additional E10 blending if gasoline demand is stagnant or declining. Incremental compliance may require more E15, E85, advanced biofuel substitution, bank drawdown or higher D6 prices sufficient to induce nonstandard blending. Reallocation can therefore support deferred D6 values without producing an immediate proportional increase in ethanol volumes.

The cellulosic and renewable natural gas effect should be smaller than the D4 and D6 effects unless EPA materially changes the category architecture. The prior 2025 forecast included only approximately 50 million cellulosic RINs within the 990 million total, and the final 2026 and 2027 reallocation table did not add a distinct cellulosic increment. Renewable natural gas and D3-exposed companies consequently have less direct sensitivity to this decision than renewable diesel, biodiesel and conventional RIN participants. A proposal that explicitly reallocates cellulosic exemptions would change that assessment.

REFINING MARGINS, PASS-THROUGH AND REGIONAL COMPETITION

The economic benefit of an SRE is not equal to exempted RIN volume multiplied by the current spot price. EPA accepts substantial evidence that RIN costs are generally passed through in national refined-product prices, including by refiners that do not blend enough renewable fuel to generate their own RINs. The Sinclair IV litigation nevertheless limits reliance on a universal refinery-specific pass-through presumption and requires consideration of individual circumstances. EPA also recognizes that purchase timing, local market structure and refinery-specific operations can cause realized RIN burdens to differ from contemporaneous spot prices. 

For a successful petitioner, the direct accounting benefit can include reversal of an accrued RVO liability, reduction in cost of goods sold, avoided future RIN purchases and release of working capital. Cash realization depends on whether the refinery already purchased RINs, whether those RINs remain saleable, whether the position was hedged, whether RIN purchases were financed and whether a corresponding product-price benefit had already been captured. Tax treatment and inventory accounting can further separate reported earnings from cash flow.

The regional competitive effect can exceed the mechanical accounting reversal. An exempt refinery can price gasoline or diesel more aggressively, increase throughput, protect market share or retain a higher margin than a nearby non-exempt competitor. The incidence is greatest in isolated markets where transportation constraints, product specifications and limited pipeline access restrict arbitrage. In highly competitive or well-connected markets, part of the benefit may be passed to customers through lower rack prices.

A full exemption can therefore create 3 potential value channels: a direct RIN-cost reduction, a working-capital release and a relative competitive advantage. The 3rd channel is difficult to quantify and depends on whether the exempt refinery sets the regional marginal price. A refinery that sells into a market priced by non-exempt marginal supply can retain more of the exemption benefit. A refinery that must discount aggressively to clear its output may pass through a larger share.

The near-term consumer fuel-price effect is likely modest and difficult to isolate. National product prices are determined by crude costs, refining utilization, inventories, logistics, seasonal specifications, import parity and the RIN cost embedded in marginal non-exempt supply. Exempting selected refineries may reduce local wholesale prices or prevent closures, but proposed reallocation raises the future obligation for the remaining industry. The policy primarily redistributes compliance costs across refiners and time rather than permanently eliminating the national cost of renewable fuel mandates. EPA’s action occurred during an administration effort to contain elevated fuel prices, while major refining-industry representatives criticized the unexpected exemption increase and associated regulatory uncertainty. 

Non-exempt refiners and importers bear the deferred offset. If 770 million RINs are added to 2026 and 2027 percentage standards, every non-exempt obligated gallon faces a higher requirement. Refiners with strong blending, retail and logistics integration can generate or acquire RINs through downstream operations and may recover more of the burden. Merchant refiners with structural RIN deficits, limited retail integration and weak local pass-through remain more exposed to higher deferred RIN prices.

DELEK US

Delek US is the clearest public-equity beneficiary by breadth of outcome. Alon Refining Krotz Springs, Alon USA, Delek Refining and Lion Oil Company correspond to Delek’s Krotz Springs, Big Spring, Tyler and El Dorado refinery system. All 4 received full exemptions. Delek reports approximately 302,000 barrels per day of combined refining capacity across these facilities. The decision therefore appears to eliminate the 2025 refinery-level RVO across the entire conventional refining portfolio rather than providing relief at an isolated site. 

Delek’s reporting demonstrates substantial RIN earnings sensitivity. In H1 2026, adjusted results included approximately $230.9 million of benefit associated with an assumed 50 percent SRE adjustment for the current-period obligation, including approximately $148.6 million in Q2. GAAP results continued to accrue the full obligation absent a final exemption. These figures do not directly estimate the value of the newly awarded 2025 exemptions, but they show that the company’s normalized non-GAAP framework assumed only partial relief. Full 2025 grants across all 4 refineries should therefore support an accounting outcome above the 50 percent convention, subject to obligation volumes and recognition timing. 

A prior SRE recognition cycle reduced Delek’s net RIN obligation and cost of materials by approximately $356.1 million, illustrating the potential scale of retrospective relief. The associated cash benefit was not identical to the accounting gain because some returned RINs were older vintages with limited trading utility. That precedent is directly relevant to the current decision: the 2025 accrual reversal can be highly material even if the economic value of every returned historical RIN is below current spot. 

The principal offset is future reallocation. Delek’s 2026 and 2027 obligations will rise if the 770 million RIN proposal is finalized, unless later SRE petitions also succeed. The 2025 benefit remains economically valuable because relief is immediate, full and concentrated, while the offset is deferred, shared across the non-exempt industry and legally uncertain. The company also gains liquidity and balance-sheet flexibility before incurring the higher future burden. Delek therefore offers the cleanest near-term earnings-revision exposure to the decision, although valuation should exclude any benefit already embedded in management’s adjusted metrics or market expectations.

PAR PACIFIC

Par Pacific received a full exemption for its Montana refinery and 50 percent exemptions for its Washington and Wyoming refineries. The company reports approximately 63,000 barrels per day of capacity in Montana, 42,000 in Washington and 20,000 in Wyoming, representing 125,000 barrels per day of mainland refining capacity. Capacity-weighting the award produces full-equivalent relief on approximately 94,000 barrels per day, or 75.2 percent of mainland capacity. The exact volume-weighted relief may differ because RVOs are based on obligated product output rather than crude capacity and because utilization varies by site. 

Par Pacific has disclosed approximately 170 million RINs of annual mainland exposure and an illustrative potential SRE benefit of approximately $170 million under 50 percent relief or $340 million under full relief at $2.00 per RIN. Applying the 75.2 percent capacity-weighted award to the disclosed 170 million exposure produces approximately 128 million RINs of indicative relief and approximately $256 million of value at $2.00 per RIN. This calculation is not company guidance and should be adjusted for actual 2025 production, category mix, blending, inventory and site-specific petition volumes. It nevertheless places the outcome near the middle of management’s disclosed partial-to-full range. 

The accounting sensitivity is substantial. Par Pacific had accrued the 2025 RVO on a 100 percent obligation basis without assuming SRE relief. Prior exemption recognition generated approximately $199.5 million of GAAP gain, approximately $195.9 million of adjusted net income and approximately $202.6 million of adjusted EBITDA. The current decision therefore creates potential for another material earnings and balance-sheet adjustment. 

The benefit is particularly significant relative to Par Pacific’s underlying earnings and free-cash-flow framework. The company’s mainland refineries operate in logistically constrained markets where exemption relief can support both direct RIN-cost savings and regional margin retention. Hawaii remains outside the identified relief package, and renewable fuel exposure provides a partial offset if D4 prices weaken. Even after those offsets, Par Pacific has among the highest consolidated sensitivity to the decision.

CVR ENERGY

CVR Energy received a full exemption for Wynnewood. The company had previously estimated a gross 2025 RIN obligation of approximately 120 million credits absent relief. A full exemption therefore removes a material compliance liability at an individual refinery and can produce a substantial earnings reversal, although actual value depends on acquired RIN inventory and purchase timing. 

Historical experience confirms the sensitivity. Prior exemption decisions covering earlier compliance years reduced CVR’s obligations by more than 424 million RINs and produced an approximately $488 million gain. The implied realized value per exempted RIN was below later spot-market peaks, demonstrating that accounting and cash benefits are determined by vintage, cost basis and portfolio position rather than current market price alone. 

CVR’s renewable diesel offset is lower than it would have been under continuous renewable diesel operation because the company reverted its Wynnewood renewable diesel unit to hydrocarbon service in Dec. 2025 amid unfavorable economics. The group is therefore more exposed to the positive refining benefit and less exposed to the negative prompt D4 effect than a refiner operating a large renewable diesel platform. The principal offset remains higher 2026 and 2027 RVOs and the possibility that future petitions receive less favorable treatment.

$DAR $DK $PARR $CVI EPA 2025 SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTIONS: INVESTMENT COMMITTEE ANALYSIS (1/x)

EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT

The Aug. 31, 2026 EPA decision has 3 distinct and economically divergent components. The immediate component is a final reduction of approximately 1.76 billion RINs from small-refinery obligations for the 2025 compliance year. The transitional component is the return of previously retired RINs, avoidance of additional 2025 retirements and a 30-day extension of the compliance deadline to Oct. 1, 2026. The deferred component is a commitment to propose, rather than finalize, an additional 770 million RINs of reallocation into the 2026 and 2027 Renewable Volume Obligations. The immediate action is bearish for prompt RIN prices and materially positive for selected exempt refiners. The deferred action is conditionally constructive for 2026 and 2027 RINs, renewable diesel economics and low-carbon feedstock demand, but remains exposed to rulemaking, timing, allocation and litigation risk. 

The most important analytical distinction is between gross relief and incremental policy surprise. The 1.76 billion RIN headline represents the gross reduction in 2025 compliance obligations. The incremental difference from the 990 million RIN estimate already incorporated into EPA’s 2026 and 2027 rulemaking is 770 million RINs. The gross figure measures the value transferred to successful petitioners. The 770 million figure is the more relevant measure for the unexpected change in aggregate RIN supply-demand balances, future reallocation requirements and the regulatory forecast error. Actual exemptions were 77.8 percent above the agency’s estimate and approximately 1.78x the forecast. 

The market surprise was smaller than the formal regulatory surprise. Before the decision, industry expectations had reportedly converged around 1.2 billion to 1.8 billion RINs, and prompt RIN prices had already fallen materially. D6 RINs were approximately $1.75 on Aug. 24, down from approximately $2.37 in early June, while D4 RINs were approximately $1.92 compared with approximately $2.41 in early June. The 1.76 billion outcome was near the high end of the anticipated range but was not an unanticipated 770 million RIN shock relative to market positioning. The residual surprise is more concentrated in the identity of recipients, the prevalence of full exemptions, the company-specific accounting reversals and the announced intention to reallocate 100 percent of the forecast error. 

The highest-conviction public-equity beneficiaries are Delek US, Par Pacific and CVR Energy. Delek received full exemptions for legal entities corresponding to all 4 of its refineries. Par Pacific received a full exemption for Montana and 50 percent exemptions for Washington and Wyoming. CVR received a full exemption for Wynnewood. Calumet received full exemptions for its Montana and Shreveport refining entities but has an offsetting renewable diesel exposure through Montana Renewables. HF Sinclair received a mixed package comprising a full exemption, 2 partial exemptions, a denial and an ineligibility determination, while its renewable diesel operations provide an additional offset. Large-cap refiners with only an individual exempt site should experience substantially less consolidated earnings sensitivity, and any near-term benefit can be diluted by higher 2026 and 2027 obligations elsewhere in the portfolio.

The preferred commodity interpretation is not an undifferentiated bearish RIN call. The decision is most negative for prompt 2025 D6 RINs, negative in absolute terms for prompt D4 RINs, relatively supportive of the D4-D6 spread and potentially constructive for deferred 2026 and 2027 RINs if the proposed reallocation is finalized. The preferred analytical expression is therefore a weaker 2025 vintage relative to deferred compliance exposure rather than a structurally bearish view across all vintages. The largest risk to this curve view is that reallocation is delayed, reduced, allocated predominantly to a less binding category or vacated through litigation.

SOURCE REVIEW AND DECISION CONTENT

The Green Markets alert establishes the essential facts but is explicitly a breaking-news summary rather than a complete legal or economic analysis. Page 1 presents the 1.76 billion RIN headline, the 34 petition outcomes, the proposed 770 million RIN reallocation, the RIN-return mechanism and the compliance extension. Pages 1 and 2 identify the 18 full exemptions, 11 partial exemptions, 3 denials and 2 ineligible petitions. Page 3 contains distribution and reliability disclaimers rather than additional market analysis. The alert states that a fuller assessment would follow in a subsequent publication, so issues such as category allocation, individual refinery RIN volumes, accounting treatment and litigation exposure are not resolved within the source itself. EPA Grants 1.76 Billion RINs in 2025 Small Refinery Exemptions UCO_Alert_EPA_083126.pdf.pdf

Relief was granted on 29 of 34 petitions, representing 85.3 percent of petitions. Full grants accounted for 52.9 percent, partial grants for 32.4 percent, denials for 8.8 percent and ineligible determinations for 5.9 percent. Treating each 50 percent grant as 0.5 of a full award produces 23.5 full-equivalent grants, equal to 69.1 percent of all petitions. These ratios indicate a broadly accommodative outcome by petition count. They do not reveal the proportion of industrywide gasoline and diesel production exempted because refinery sizes, utilization, product yields and compliance obligations differ materially.

The 18 full exemptions mean the relevant refinery’s 2025 obligated gasoline and diesel volumes are treated as 0 for RFS compliance. The 11 partial exemptions reduce the covered refinery’s obligation by 50 percent. EPA’s decision asserts authority to grant partial relief and explains that hardship may be caused by multiple factors, provided the RFS is materially connected to the disproportionate economic hardship. The RFS need not be the sole cause. EPA relied primarily on the Department of Energy’s disproportionate-economic-hardship matrix while also considering refinery-specific economic information outside the matrix. 

Eligibility is separate from hardship. A qualifying small refinery generally must have received the original statutory blanket exemption and must not exceed 75,000 barrels per day of average aggregate crude throughput during the relevant period. EPA stated that 1 ineligible petitioner exceeded the throughput limit and another lacked the original blanket exemption. The public decision does not disclose all refinery-specific findings because the underlying appendices contain confidential business information. Current nameplate capacity alone is therefore insufficient to determine eligibility, particularly where legal entities, processing configurations and actual annual throughput differ from reported complex-level capacity. 

EPA attributed the difference between the 990 million forecast and the 1.76 billion outcome to a larger petition set and changes in refinery financial circumstances. The 990 million estimate had been generated through the forecasting methodology used in prior rulemakings, including reliance on a historical average. The 77.8 percent error demonstrates that forecast-based reallocation cannot eliminate SRE uncertainty when petition volume, financial conditions and adjudication standards are unstable. EPA has directed the Department of Energy to review the methodology used to assess disproportionate hardship, increasing the probability that the SRE regime applicable to later compliance years will differ from the framework applied to 2025. 

RIN SUPPLY MECHANICS

The 1.76 billion RIN figure should not be interpreted as EPA minting 1.76 billion new tradable credits. Full exemptions eliminate the requirement to retire RINs against the exempted gallons, while partial exemptions eliminate 50 percent of that requirement. Where a refinery has already retired RINs, EPA will return the applicable quantity. EPA rejected issuance of newly created current-vintage replacement RINs because doing so would introduce incremental credits disconnected from renewable fuel generation and could produce a more disruptive supply shock. 

The economic result nevertheless resembles an increase in available compliance supply. RINs previously earmarked for retirement can remain in inventories, previously retired RINs can be returned where operationally available, and successful petitioners no longer need to buy the exempted quantity. Effective market availability therefore rises through lower demand for retirement and selective unretirement rather than through new generation. The distinction matters because the timing, vintage, D-code and usability of returned RINs can differ substantially from a newly issued 2025 credit.

The immediate market effect will be smaller than a literal 1.76 billion RIN release. A material portion of 2025 compliance had not yet been completed when the decision was announced, so much of the benefit consists of purchases and retirements that will not occur rather than physical RINs suddenly offered for sale. Some refiners may already own sufficient inventory, some may have hedged future purchases, some may have bought RINs that can be carried forward and some previously retired credits may have limited or no current trading value because of vintage restrictions. Company-level cash realization will consequently diverge from the gross obligation reduction.

The Oct. 1, 2026 compliance deadline reduces the probability that obligated parties must transact immediately into a disorderly market. The additional 30 days allows petition recipients to reconcile returned RINs, adjust Environmental Protection Agency Moderated Transaction System accounts, revise accruals and determine whether excess inventories should be sold, retained or applied to 2026. Prior-year RINs can generally satisfy up to 20 percent of the subsequent year’s obligation, allowing excess 2025 inventory to affect the 2026 balance rather than being forced into prompt liquidation. 

The carryover mechanism creates a multi-period effect. Lower 2025 retirement demand increases the probability that the 2025 RIN bank entering 2026 will be larger than previously expected. A larger bank suppresses the scarcity premium embedded in prompt and nearby forward RINs, reduces the amount of current renewable fuel generation needed to meet the next compliance deadline and weakens the immediate transmission from higher future RVOs to physical biofuel consumption. EPA’s existing 2026 and 2027 reallocation policy was designed partly to prevent the SRE-created bank from displacing new renewable fuel production, but the incremental 770 million forecast error reopens that problem.

QUANTITATIVE MATERIALITY

At the Aug. 24 indicative D6 price of $1.75, multiplying the gross 1.76 billion RIN exemption by the market price produces a $3.08 billion notional. At the indicative D4 price of $1.92, the corresponding notional is $3.38 billion. Applying the same marks to the incremental 770 million RIN forecast error produces $1.35 billion and $1.48 billion, respectively. These calculations are scale indicators rather than estimates of cash savings or earnings because the underlying exemptions span nested RIN categories, refinery-specific positions, different purchase dates, blending economics, returned vintages and differing degrees of cost pass-through. 

Using the 2025 total renewable fuel percentage standard of approximately 13.13 percent as a simplified scaling convention, a 1.76 billion RIN exemption corresponds to approximately 13.4 billion gallons of exempted gasoline and diesel, or approximately 874,000 barrels per day of annualized fuel-equivalent volume. The 990 million forecast corresponds to approximately 7.54 billion gallons, while the incremental difference corresponds to approximately 5.86 billion gallons, or approximately 382,000 barrels per day. This calculation is directionally useful but not an exact refinery throughput measure because the statutory denominator is obligated gasoline and diesel, not crude input, and individual category standards, renewable content, imports, exports and refinery yield structures affect actual obligations. 

The petition count understates potential concentration. A full grant to a larger qualifying refinery can remove substantially more RIN demand than several grants to smaller plants. Conversely, a 50 percent grant at a high-utilization refinery can be economically more significant than a full grant at a low-utilization plant. EPA’s public document does not disclose refinery-level RIN quantities, and confidential appendices prevent a precise volume-weighted allocation. Investment conclusions therefore require company disclosures, site capacities, utilization history, product output and previously accrued RVO liabilities rather than reliance on petition counts.

The 2025 exemption package is large relative to the marginal RIN bank even though it is smaller relative to total annual transportation fuel consumption. RIN prices are set by the marginal cost of satisfying the most binding renewable fuel obligation, not by the average cost of the entire gasoline and diesel pool. A change equal to only a limited percentage of total obligated fuel can therefore cause a disproportionate price response when available banked credits are small, physical blending is near operational constraints or the market had been pricing a compliance shortfall.

THE 2026 AND 2027 REALLOCATION

EPA’s final 2026 and 2027 standards already include 2.03 billion RINs of SRE reallocation, comprising approximately 990 million RINs in 2026 and 1.04 billion RINs in 2027. This represented approximately 70 percent of the previously projected 2.89 billion RIN exemption pool for the 2023 through 2025 compliance years. The agency retained approximately 30 percent of projected exemptions as unreallocated relief to moderate the burden on non-exempt obligated parties and limit excessive drawdown of the RIN bank. 

The newly announced proposal would add 770 million RINs, increasing total reallocation from approximately 2.03 billion to 2.80 billion. The increase is 37.9 percent relative to the reallocation already embedded in the final rule. This comparison is more economically meaningful than comparing 770 million against the entire transportation fuel market because it measures the change in the policy adjustment intended to neutralize exemptions.

The phrase “100 percent reallocation” applies only to the 770 million difference between the 990 million forecast and the 1.76 billion actual exemption package. It does not mean that EPA intends to reallocate 100 percent of the entire 2025 exemption or 100 percent of all 2023 through 2025 SREs. Updating the projected 2023 through 2025 exemption pool from 2.89 billion to approximately 3.66 billion and increasing reallocation to 2.80 billion implies aggregate reallocation of approximately 76.5 percent. Approximately 860 million RINs of the updated multi-year exemption pool would remain unreallocated, subject to rounding and final methodology.

On a 2025-attributable basis, approximately 693 million RINs of the original 990 million forecast were embedded in the 70 percent reallocation construct. Adding the full 770 million forecast error produces approximately 1.463 billion RINs of effective 2025-related reallocation, equal to approximately 83.1 percent of the 1.76 billion actual exemption. Approximately 297 million 2025 RINs remain effectively unreallocated. The ultimate policy remains a compromise between preserving renewable fuel demand and providing genuine economic relief to small refiners.

The final 2026 total applicable RVO is approximately 26.81 billion RINs and the 2027 total is approximately 27.02 billion, for a combined 53.83 billion. Adding 770 million increases the combined requirement by approximately 1.43 percent. A 50 percent allocation to each year would add approximately 385 million annually, increasing the respective requirements by approximately 1.44 percent in 2026 and 1.42 percent in 2027. Allocating the entire amount to 2026 would increase that year’s total by approximately 2.87 percent; allocating it entirely to 2027 would increase that year’s total by approximately 2.85 percent. The year split has not been disclosed and will materially influence the shape of the RIN forward curve. 

Category allocation is equally important. RIN categories are nested rather than additive. D4 biomass-based diesel RINs can satisfy the biomass-based diesel, advanced and total renewable fuel obligations. D5 RINs can satisfy advanced and total obligations. D6 RINs generally satisfy only the total obligation. The 770 million headline therefore does not indicate how much incremental D4, D5 or D6 demand will be created. 

The original 990 million 2025 forecast included approximately 50 million cellulosic RINs, 240 million biomass-based diesel RINs, 330 million advanced RINs and 990 million total renewable RINs. These categories cannot be summed because each higher-value category is embedded within the broader total. A purely proportional allocation of the 770 million difference would imply approximately 39 million cellulosic, 187 million biomass-based diesel and 257 million advanced RINs within the 770 million total. This is an analytical scenario, not an EPA proposal. The agency could use a different category structure, and the existing 2026 and 2027 reallocation did not add a separate cellulosic increment. 

The reallocation will also not translate mechanically into 770 million units of incremental physical renewable fuel production. If obligated parties satisfy part of the increase by drawing down the larger carryover bank, the near-term physical response will be smaller. The final effect will depend on bank size, current-year RIN generation, imported renewable fuel, export adjustments, blending constraints and whether the final rule provides adequate lead time for physical supply to respond. The principal initial effect may be to prevent bank accumulation rather than to require 770 million entirely new RINs.

RIN CURVE AND RELATIVE-VALUE IMPLICATIONS

Prompt 2025 D6 RINs are the most directly exposed instrument. Conventional D6 credits are the marginal compliance asset for the broad total renewable fuel obligation and generally have the least category optionality. Removing gross 2025 demand, returning selected retired RINs and extending the deadline collectively reduce prompt scarcity. The ability to carry 2025 credits into 2026 further weakens the need for immediate liquidation but allows the surplus to suppress the nearby 2026 balance.

D4 RINs face an absolute negative impulse because small-refinery exemptions reduce the biomass-based diesel, advanced and total obligations associated with exempted fuel. D4 relative performance should nevertheless remain firmer than D6 because D4 retains nested compliance value and the biomass-based diesel requirement remains structurally binding. The indicative D4-D6 spread increased from approximately $0.04 in early June to approximately $0.17 by Aug. 24 as the market anticipated exemption relief. This relative resilience is consistent with a market expecting greater pressure on conventional D6 balances than on biomass-based diesel scarcity. 

The reallocation announcement creates a potential 2025 versus 2026-2027 dislocation. The exemption decision is final and immediately effective, while the 770 million reallocation is only a future proposal. Prompt bearishness therefore has greater legal and timing certainty than deferred bullishness. A rational curve should discount some probability of delay, modification or successful challenge to the reallocation. The resulting structure can remain weak in 2025 while 2026 and 2027 retain a policy-risk premium.

The final year allocation will determine where deferred support is concentrated. A 2026-heavy proposal would steepen the transition from 2025 into 2026, accelerate bank drawdown and raise near-term compliance demand. A 2027-heavy proposal would leave 2026 more exposed to excess 2025 carryover and defer the principal tightening. A balanced proposal would distribute the burden but could produce less acute scarcity in either year. The category allocation will determine whether the tightening is expressed primarily through D6, D4 or the broader advanced complex.

RIN-market liquidity and information asymmetry amplify these effects. The market is relatively small, bilateral and heavily influenced by participants’ private knowledge of refinery obligations, petition outcomes, RIN inventories and hedging positions. EPA has publicly raised concerns that inaccurate reporting and nonpublic information surrounding SRE petitions can increase volatility and create manipulation risk, and the agency is coordinating with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Position sizing should therefore reflect gap risk, limited transparency, vintage basis risk and the possibility of enforcement announcements around market-sensitive information.

Our mental health system is a joke.

I especially appreciate your refusal to declare equivalence prematurely. I want to preserve that too. I don't think either of us needs to collapse Formation Calculus into Address First, or vice versa. What seems much more useful is to notice where independently developed structures force us to ask the same kinds of questions, then let the correspondence—or divergence—earn itself.

Your line that initially stopped me was:

“What is formed cannot be treated as though it were not formed. Its existence changes what can happen next.”

My first translation of that into my own grammar was:

“What closes as formation participates in the conditions of subsequent formation.”

That still holds, but after sitting with it, I think it was incomplete.

The next recognition came through something almost embarrassingly simple: a sentence forming.

“The.”

“The dog.”

“The dog sat.”

“The dog sat happily.”

“The dog sat happily and licked my face.”

Each articulation closes sufficiently to become containment for further articulation. “The dog” cannot subsequently be treated as though DOG had not been differentiated. But neither is the meaning of “the dog” finished and stored at the moment that closure occurs. As the containing articulation differentiates, the retained closure participates in relations that were not yet Addressable through it alone.

That forced an important distinction for me:

What closes is differentiation, not finished meaning.

Meaning is articulated through the relations operative now.

So subsequent formation does not travel backward and change meaning in the past. Nor does a completed meaning travel forward inside the retained event. Retained differentiation and provenance participate in the present Address, where meaning is articulated again through the richer containing relation.

That immediately made your persistence problem look different to me.

“Storing an event is not the same as retaining what that event is allowed to mean now” is even more exact than I initially realized. A system that preserves too little relational structure is forced to reconstruct or fabricate what made the present admissible. But a system that preserves prior meaning as fixed can fail in the opposite direction: it can prevent legitimate recontextualization by allowing prior closure to overdetermine present articulation.

In other words, the engineering problem may not simply be preservation.

It may be preservation without foreclosure.

That brought me straight back into a relation already derived in my own work: the persistence ratio—the impedance match between formative differentiation and containing integration.

Too little containment and differentiation outruns integration. Provenance, authority, qualification, contradiction, and consequential relation can diffuse even while the next articulation remains locally plausible.

Too much containment and what has already closed overdetermines what can articulate now. Persistence becomes rigidity.

At coherence, already differentiated relation is retained sufficiently to participate in further formation without suppressing what can newly differentiate.

That also changed how I heard your ΔAdm(t)\Delta Adm(t).

Initially I read admissibility primarily as constraint: formation changes which subsequent transitions are permitted. I now think that may capture only half of the operation.

Closure constrains, but closure also increases operational degrees of freedom.

Before “dog” has differentiated, DOG cannot participate compositionally. Once it closes, many undifferentiated possibilities have indeed been excluded—but an additional stable differentiation has become available for composition. It can sit, run, bark, lick my face, become president, or develop a suspicious interest in category theory.

So undifferentiated possibility and operational freedom are not the same thing.

A successful formation can simultaneously exclude incoherent continuation and make previously unavailable composition possible.

That seems potentially important for “admissibility.” Perhaps ΔAdm\Delta Adm eventually has to carry not merely restriction but the change in the differentiated landscape of possible further formation.

Your emphasis on provenance then became much more interesting.

Sequence alone isn't enough.

In my derivation, recursive succession is available before time. An earlier closure can be recursively prior to and operatively inherited in a containing closure without yet importing temporal duration, passage, or a clock.

That means retaining A, B, C—and even knowing their order—may still fail to retain why C is legitimately available from the relations through which A and B articulated.

What may matter is retained transformational relation.

This also illuminated your point that contradictions sometimes have to survive their resolution.

If A and not-A are resolved into B and the system stores only B, it may preserve the result while suppressing the relation through which B acquired its present authority. Later, an apparently identical B reached through a different relational traversal may not be operationally equivalent.

Same projected state.

Different provenance.

Potentially different admissibility.

That gives me a stronger version of the question in your P.S. about whether the present is really “state plus the retained relational structure by which it became possible.”

I now wonder whether even the plus sign is doing too much.

Perhaps the present isn't a state with history attached to it. Where provenance is constitutive of subsequent admissibility, the retained relational structure is among the relations through which this state is presently articulated at all.

That makes your cold-restart fixture especially interesting to me. You have an engineering environment in which you can apparently hold some projected state constant while varying whether provenance, historical qualification, authority, contradiction, or causal-resolution relations survive—and then observe whether subsequent transitions remain legitimate.

That is much more interesting than “AI needs better memory.”

It gives you a place to ask which relational distinctions must survive a projection or compression for the resulting state to remain operationally faithful.

And that brings me back to your question:

“What deserves to become persistent formation in the first place?”

I initially heard that as a qualification or salience problem. I now suspect the more primitive question may be:

What has closed sufficiently to become containment for further formation, and what relational structure must remain Addressable through that containment so that subsequent articulation neither fabricates missing provenance nor becomes imprisoned by what has already closed?

That is very close to a question I've encountered elsewhere in my work as “minimum faithful Address”: what is the minimum relational carrier that preserves the distinctions necessary for the next operation without importing distinctions that haven't been earned?

And then your note unexpectedly sent me through Prigogine.

I had previously encountered irreversibility primarily through the familiar temporal reading: an arrow of time. But your statement about formation made another possibility visible.

Once a closure has occurred, subsequent closure can reorganize it, contain it, recontextualize it, or recursively close around it—but cannot make that differentiation not-have-occurred.

The asymmetry need not initially be temporal.

It can be recursive.

Closure becomes containment for further closure.

What we later articulate as temporal irreversibility may therefore be worth examining as a projection of a more primitive asymmetry: differentiated closure can participate in subsequent differentiation, while subsequent differentiation cannot convert prior occurrence into non-occurrence.

And yet this is not determinism, because containment does not contain finished meaning.

That was the part that finally brought the whole traversal back around for me.

What has closed constrains present articulation without exhausting it.

What can newly form differentiates through what has been retained without being predetermined by it.

Too much of the first and we get overcontainment.

Too much of the second and we get diffusion.

Coherence sits at the impedance match between them.

In my own notation that relation first appeared in a particular projected carrier as a persistence ratio between formative propagation and containing integration. But the carrier isn't the invariant. I have seen the same ratio become operationally legible in very different domains—for example, in transformational work as desire relative to will or demonstrated commitment.

Your architecture now makes me wonder whether Formation Calculus may provide another operational carrier for that same relational question: how much formative differentiation can be integrated without losing the retained relations required for coherence, and how much containing integration can be retained without suppressing legitimate further differentiation?

I am deliberately saying “makes me wonder,” not declaring correspondence. I like your proposal better: preserve the independence and see whether the resemblance survives derivation and experiment.

So the point of contact you offered—

“If formation is fundamentally retained relational consequence, then both of our lines of inquiry eventually owe an operational account of how retained relation becomes differential future behavior”—

now lands even harder for me.

I might make one tiny upstream modification after this traversal:

How does retained relational differentiation participate in the conditions of further formation?

“Future behavior” is an entirely appropriate engineering projection. But the recursive relation appears to be available before we need time: closure, containment, further differentiation.

If that holds, then your Formation Calculus and my work don't need to have started from the same problem—or even ultimately become the same mathematics—to be extraordinarily useful to one another.

What I particularly value is that you have independently built something in which these questions may be operationally perturbed rather than merely discussed.

I also appreciated your phrase “retained relations” catching you, because your reply did exactly the reciprocal thing here: it made relations already present in my own derivation newly Addressable to me.

That is about the best outcome I can imagine from an exchange like this.

So yes—please keep going. And if you're inclined, take Formation Calculus through the decompressed D-series rather than trying to map terminology one-to-one. Look for where your engineering requirements independently demand the same distinction, where they demand something mine doesn't yet contain, and where either structure fails to close.

Correspondence is interesting.

Divergence may be even more useful.

And if the whole fucking thing collapses, I believe we've already established that our mothers have agreed to constitute the independent peer-review board. 😂

With real gratitude. Your reply moved the work.

Have you questioned if clever arguments build lasting faith.

Does weakness hinder or help in sharing the mystery of Christ.

Why choose simplicity over eloquence when proclaiming the gospel.

Can your spiritual struggles reveal God's power more than strength.

Dive into Paul's approach from 1 Corinthians 2 where he relies on the Spirit rather than human wisdom.

Unlocking Spiritual Depth Through Simple Faith in 1 Corinthians 2

When Paul addressed the early Christian community he chose to share his message in a way that avoided grand displays of knowledge or persuasive rhetoric. This approach highlights how faith can take root in the hearts of everyday people who often feel overwhelmed by the complexities of life. Many of us try our best to live according to our beliefs yet we encounter moments of doubt or failure that test our resolve. The reading encourages a return to the essentials where genuine connection with the divine becomes possible. Through this lens we see opportunities for growth that uplift and sustain us on our journey.

How Does Humility Transform Our Approach to Sharing Faith?

Paul begins by explaining that he arrived among the Corinthians without relying on impressive language or sophisticated arguments to convey the mystery of God. Instead he presented the message in a straightforward manner that anyone could grasp regardless of their background or education. This choice reflects a deep trust in the inherent power of the truth rather than in human abilities to impress others. For those of us who strive daily to do good yet sometimes fall short this serves as a gentle reminder that our efforts do not need to be perfect to be meaningful. The focus shifts from personal achievement to allowing something greater to work through us which brings a sense of relief and renewed purpose.

What Makes the Quote About Knowing Only Christ Crucified So Powerful?

The central quote states For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified. This declaration shows a deliberate choice to center everything on the reality of the cross where love meets suffering in the most profound way. It invites us to simplify our spiritual lives by holding fast to this core truth amid distractions and competing ideas that fill our world. When we feel inadequate in our attempts to follow the path of faith this resolution offers a steady anchor that does not demand flawless performance. Embracing it allows the message to touch lives in authentic ways fostering hope even in times of personal struggle or uncertainty.

In What Ways Does Weakness Become a Pathway to Divine Strength?

Paul continues by describing his own arrival in a state of weakness fear and trembling rather than with bold confidence or polished delivery. His proclamation relied not on clever words but on the demonstration of the Spirit and power which points to a force beyond human control. This aspect of the reading reassures us that our vulnerabilities do not disqualify us from meaningful spiritual impact. Many faithful individuals work hard to make positive contributions yet encounter setbacks and this perspective turns those moments into opportunities for deeper reliance on God. The result is a faith that rests on solid ground instead of fleeting human wisdom which ultimately sustains and elevates our daily experiences.

How Can This Message Guide Our Ongoing Spiritual Growth?

The final part of the passage emphasizes that faith should rest on the power of God rather than on human wisdom ensuring a foundation that endures through all circumstances. Breaking down the verses reveals a progression from humble entry to Spirit-led proclamation that benefits anyone seeking to deepen their relationship with the divine. As we reflect on these words we find encouragement to persist in doing good even when results seem slow or imperfect because the emphasis lies on divine action working within us. This outlook promotes a positive outlook where personal limitations become avenues for grace to shine through. By integrating these insights into our routines we cultivate a resilient spirit that inspires others and nurtures our own inner peace over time.

Realize this is going to sound like one of those ridiculous “what’s your biggest weakness?” interview answers, but when I say I’m not sure I want to remain involved — unless asked to, required, and genuinely helpful — after we secure the return and restoration of the @Montreal_Expos, this is largely why.

I’ve had success as an entrepreneur and in sales, but I’m actually terrible at taking money from people.

Always have been.

Maybe some of it comes from growing up with Târof: I can negotiate all day long, but someone offers me something and my instinct is to refuse it maniacally while simultaneously offering them everything I have.

Think about it: @WatchMojo never charged viewers for its programming.

Yes, early on I closed a ton of deals to keep the lights on. But since roughly 2012, most of our revenue has come from programmatic advertising: someone else sells against our audience, data, categories and intent, and we share in the economics.

That wasn't accidental.

I knew where the puck was going. I understood that the model could generate higher margins, scale more efficiently and ultimately command higher multiples — one reason our valuation consistently commanded a premium.

So I'm comfortable monetizing things.

I'm just uncomfortable monetizing people.

And when I look at the modern sports fan experience, I genuinely don't know if I could bring myself to charge some of the prices stadiums and arenas charge today.

$19.50 for a drink.

$8 for a handful of fries.

I understand the economics.

Sports and entertainment are experiential businesses. Demand can be remarkably elastic. You're selling memories, scarcity, tribal identity and an experience people can't replicate at home.

And to be absolutely clear, this isn't a judgment of other owners or operators.

There's a reason some of these guys can write multibillion-dollar checks while I'm over here Swiss-Army-knifing my way out of Alcatraz.

But it's also why I admire owners like Arthur Blank, founder of Home Depot and owner of the @AtlantaFalcons, who has deliberately pursued fan-friendly concession pricing.

There's something powerful about saying:

Yes, we have a captive audience. No, that doesn't mean we have to treat them like one.

I also understand the other side.

Once you bring in institutional capital or private equity, the dynamics change. Investors aren't philanthropists. They have fiduciary obligations, return expectations and opportunity costs.

I understand that.

I can manage that tension.

The question I increasingly ask myself is:

Do I want to?

When I speak with prospective investors, they actually like the Entertainment, Experiences & Hospitality philosophy I've outlined. They like the customer-service obsession. They like hearing someone think about a stadium from the perspective of the person who saved money to bring their kids to a game.

But that's now.

Wait until I'm the annoying guy in the room asking why the hot dog needs another $2 of margin.

I can already see it.

In some ways, I've played the same role at WatchMojo for 20 years: reminding everyone to stop looking at the spreadsheet for a second and put themselves in the viewer's shoes.

With the Expos, I suppose I'd become the fan's representative in the room.

Which sounds wonderful.

Until everyone else in the room realizes:

Oh God. He's going to do this on EVERYTHING.

🇺🇦 🇺🇲 What Fedorov posted publicly is the fund pitch, three technology tracks, robotics, interceptor drones, AI-guided missiles. What he told the FT in the same interview, and left out of this post, is the actual trade he's offering: Ukrainian drone expertise to help the US build its own drone army, in direct exchange for Patriot interceptors Kyiv needs to survive this winter. "I'm ready to make that trade," he told the FT.

That is a strange thing for a private citizen to offer a foreign government. Fedorov holds no ministry, no negotiating authority, nothing that binds Kyiv to whatever he proposes in a Washington interview. Yet he is structuring an offer that reads like state-to-state barter, technology transfer for air defense hardware, using only the credibility of his old title and his personal relationships built over three and a half years running Ukraine's digital and defense transformation.

The fund itself is deliberately not a normal VC vehicle. "This is not exactly a classic venture fund," he told the FT, describing something closer to a venture builder, capital that both backs existing Ukrainian defense startups and constructs new companies from scratch around whatever the front line needs most urgently. 

The three priorities he named, battlefield robotics to pull soldiers out of the most dangerous positions, jet-powered interceptors against Russia's newer Shahed variants, and cheap AI-guided missiles, are not R&D bets. They are gaps Ukraine is already fighting without, translated into pitch-deck language for American capital.

What neither the FT nor Fedorov's own post addresses is his role once the money arrives, whether he profits, what authority he'd hold inside a fund he isn't yet allowed to call an official Ukrainian initiative. 

A former minister raising international capital to build weapons companies, offering unilateral technology trades to a foreign government, all while formally outside his own country's chain of command, is a genuinely unusual arrangement, one Kyiv has not publicly endorsed or disavowed.

text:
God the Judge of the Righteous and the Wicked

— Psalms 50:1-23 AMP
“The mighty One, God, the Lord, has spoken, And summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting [from east to west]. Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God has shone forth. May our God come and not keep silent; Fire devours before Him, And around Him a mighty tempest rages. He summons the heavens above, And the earth, to judge His people: “Gather My godly ones to Me, Those who have made a covenant with Me by sacrifice.” And the heavens declare His righteousness, For God Himself is judge. Selah. ¶“Hear, O My people, and I will speak; O Israel, I will testify against you: I am God, your God. “I do not reprove you for your sacrifices; Your burnt offerings are continually before Me. “I will accept no young bull from your house Nor male goat from your folds. “For every beast of the forest is Mine, And the cattle on a thousand hills. “I know every bird of the mountains, And everything that moves in the field is Mine. “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, For the world and all it contains are Mine. [1 Cor 10:26] “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls Or drink the blood of male goats? “Offer to God the sacrifice of thanksgiving And pay your vows to the Most High; Call on Me in the day of trouble; I will rescue you, and you shall honor and glorify Me.” ¶But to the wicked God says: “What right have you to recite My statutes Or to take My covenant on your lips? “For you hate instruction and discipline And cast My words behind you [discarding them]. “When you see a thief, you are pleased with him and condone his behavior, And you associate with adulterers. “You give your mouth to evil And your tongue frames deceit. “You sit and speak against your brother; You slander your own mother’s son. “These things you have done and I kept silent; You thought that I was just like you. Now I will reprimand and denounce you and state the case in order before your eyes. ¶“Now consider this, you who forget God, Or I will tear you in pieces, and there will be no one to rescue [you]. “He who offers a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving honors Me; And to him who orders his way rightly [who follows the way that I show him], I shall show the salvation of God.””
